 Instrumentation Amplifier vs Op Amp: Key Differences

 A single op amp can be wired as a difference amplifier in minutes, yet plenty of sensor circuits still fail in the field because that quick circuit was never the right tool for the job.

 Input Impedance

 Instrumentation Amplifier vs Op Amp comes down to internal architecture, a plain op amp needs external feedback resistors chosen by hand while an instrumentation amplifier packages that feedback internally for far higher rejection of common mode noise.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to compare Instrumentation Amplifier vs Op Amp, why a dedicated in amp chip so often outperforms a hand built difference amplifier, and when the extra cost is genuinely worth it.


 Reading the basics of a standard operational amplifier first is useful background, since an instrumentation amplifier is really three op amps working together inside one package.


 
 
 
 Instrumentation Amplifier vs Op Amp


 An operational amplifier is a general purpose gain block, the designer adds external resistors to set gain, bandwidth, and function, whether that function ends up being a difference amplifier, a filter, or a comparator.


 An instrumentation amplifier is a specialized chip built from three internal op amps in a fixed topology, with gain set by one or two external resistors and the tricky feedback paths already handled inside the package.


 Choosing between the two is really a question of how much internal engineering you want done for you before the signal ever reaches your gain setting resistor.


 How a Standard Op Amp Difference Circuit Works


 A single op amp wired as a difference amplifier uses four external resistors, and the common mode rejection of that circuit depends entirely on how well matched those four resistors actually are.


 Even one percent resistor tolerance limits common mode rejection to roughly forty six decibels, which sounds reasonable until a real sensor signal sits buried under a much larger shared noise voltage.


 Input impedance on this simple circuit is also relatively low, often around one hundred kilohms, which can load down a high impedance sensor and quietly distort the very signal being measured.


 How an Instrumentation Amplifier Is Built


 A three op amp instrumentation amplifier places a buffer stage in front of each input, giving the whole chip very high input impedance, often in the millions of ohms, regardless of the gain setting chosen.


 Those buffer stages feed a final difference stage, and because the internal resistor network is laser trimmed at the factory, common mode rejection climbs far higher than a hand matched external resistor network ever achieves.


 Gain is set with a single external resistor, so the same chip can serve a wide range of applications just by changing one component value rather than four matched ones
